newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer-diluting EMU rules risky for mkt rates.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer-diluting EMU rules risky for mkt rates.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer warned on Friday that any attempt to water down the convergence criteria for launching Europe's common currency risked forcing capital market interest rates higher.

A mere suspicion that less strict demands could be placed on potential participants in the planned launch of the Euro in January 1999 would place long-end rates at risk even today, he said in a speech to be delivered to German industrialists.

"Compromises, tricks and concessions are thus out of place. Because stability does not arise by itself, it must be ensured by choosing of particpating countries on the basis of the the criteria and by building a resilient currency union," he said.
A copy of Tietmeyer's speech was made available in advance.
Tietmeyer said it was important not to let any doubts arise as to the stability of the currency union once it was in place.

He said he was sceptical of attempts made by other countries to manipulate their finances into an acceptable shape to meet the criteria, dismissing these as "plastic surgery, which appear to have only a cosmetic function on the day."
Countries which wish to meld their currencies in the Euro from 1999 must meet certain targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt by 1997.
"The current level of convergence, especially in the area of public finances, is certainly still unsatisfactory," Tietmeyer said.

The Bundesbank president added that participants in the single currency should "agree on an additional stability pact, which has been suggested by (Finance Minister Theo) Waigel and which the Bundesbank supports."

He said Waigel was right to suggest that automatic sanctions should generally take effect for countries who fail to keep their finances under control after monetary union, but said important questions on the pact remained open.
Recent German press reports have suggested differences of opinion between the Bundesbank and Waigel on this issue.

On the domestic front, Tietmeyer urged that the social welfare system should be put onto an affordable basis for the long term, noting that wealth and income had risen sufficiently to allow a higher proportion of private cover.
